news_summary: Despite abundant hydrogen in the universe, new insights are revealing intriguing factors behind the decline in star formation.
news_summary_fr: Bien que l'hydrogène soit abondant dans l'univers, de nouvelles découvertes mettent en lumière des facteurs intrigants à l'origine du déclin de la formation stellaire.
news_summary_es: A pesar de la abundancia de hidrógeno en el universo, nuevos descubrimientos están sacando a la luz factores intrigantes que explican el descenso de la formación estelar.

articles.title: The universe has plenty of hydrogen. So why is star formation collapsing?
articles.summary: Star formation across the universe has fallen dramatically over the past 4.5 billion years, but astronomers have uncovered a surprising twist: the supply of neutral hydrogen, a key ingredient for making stars, has barely declined. Using China’s FAST radio telescope and data from roughly 2.5 million galaxies observed by DESI, researchers found that star formation was about 2.5 times higher 4.5 billion years ago, while neutral hydrogen levels were only about 1.4 times higher.
articles.content:
The universe is producing fewer stellar "babies." Over the past 4.5 billion years, the rate at which new stars form has fallen to less than half its previous level. Yet the supply of one of the most important types of "fuel" for star formation has changed surprisingly little.

That finding comes from an international research team led by scientists from the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS), working with the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) project. Using China's Five hundred meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST), the researchers made precise measurements of cosmic neutral atomic hydrogen across the past 4.5 billion years.

Their results show a striking mismatch. Star formation has declined sharply, while the amount of neutral atomic hydrogen (HI), an important reservoir of gas within galaxies, has decreased only modestly.

The findings were published online in Nature Astronomy on Sept. 1.

Why Is the Universe Making Fewer Stars?

Understanding why star formation has become less active as the universe ages is a major question in research on galaxy formation and evolution. One seemingly straightforward explanation is that galaxies have gradually consumed the cold gas needed to produce stars.

If dwindling supplies of cold gas were primarily responsible, however, astronomers would expect the dramatic fall in star formation to be accompanied by a similarly large decline in the available gas. So far, observations have not shown such a sharp depletion.

HI plays a central role in this puzzle. It is an important cold gas reservoir inside galaxies, connecting the broader cosmic supply of gas with the processes that eventually produce new stars. Astronomers primarily detect HI through its extremely faint 21-centimeter radio emission line.

Detecting that signal from distant galaxies is difficult because it is often overwhelmed by background noise.

FAST and DESI Survey Millions of Galaxies

For years, astronomers faced a major observational challenge. Very deep surveys could achieve the necessary sensitivity but could not examine large regions of the sky. Surveys covering much larger areas, meanwhile, generally lacked the sensitivity needed to detect such faint radio signals.

As a result, scientists have struggled to directly and reliably determine how the universe's total HI mass has changed across the low- to intermediate-redshift universe.

The new research tackled this problem by combining the exceptional radio sensitivity of FAST with the enormous optical spectroscopy data set provided by DESI. The team studied about 2.5 million galaxies spread across nearly one-third of the sky.

The researchers used an HI spectral stacking method to combine radio signals that would have been too faint to detect individually. Using precise measurements of each galaxy's redshift, they aligned the weak signals and stacked them together. This process allowed the average HI signal to emerge from the background noise.

The approach enabled the scientists to track changes in cosmic neutral hydrogen using a sample of unprecedented size and with exceptionally high statistical precision.

Star Formation Fell Much Faster Than Hydrogen

The results exposed a major difference between the evolution of star formation and the supply of neutral hydrogen.

About 4.5 billion years ago, the cosmic star formation rate was approximately 2.5 times higher than it is today. Over the same period, however, neutral atomic hydrogen density was only about 1.4 times higher than its present level.

In other words, star formation dropped dramatically without a comparable disappearance of the universe's HI reservoir. The findings indicate that rapidly exhausting neutral hydrogen cannot by itself explain why star formation has declined so strongly.

The Cosmic Mystery Shifts

According to the researchers, the results change the central question from "whether the gas is depleting" to "why it is increasingly difficult to form stars despite abundant neutral hydrogen reserves."

Stars do not form directly from most neutral atomic hydrogen. They are mainly born inside much denser clouds of molecular gas. Neutral atomic hydrogen occupies an important intermediate position between the universe's larger gas supply and the molecular hydrogen that can ultimately fuel star formation.

The researchers suggest that the most important changes in the more recent universe may involve how gas moves through the baryon cycle rather than how much HI exists overall.

As the flow of gas from the cosmic web becomes weaker and gas densities decrease, galaxies may become less efficient at converting HI into molecular hydrogen. Under this scenario, the overall HI reservoir can remain relatively stable while supplies of the molecular gas directly responsible for creating stars gradually decline.

Why the Universe's Star Factories Are Fading

The implications therefore extend beyond simply determining how much hydrogen exists in the universe. The findings offer an important new clue to why the universe's enormous star-forming engines have been gradually slowing down.

According to the researchers, combining observations from FAST and DESI provides a new observational benchmark for studying the cosmic gas cycle during the universe's later evolution, the long-term decline in star formation, and the broader processes shaping galaxies.

The research was led by scientists from the National Astronomical Observatories of China, the Shanghai Astronomical Observatory of CAS, and Shanghai Jiao Tong University, together with researchers participating in DESI.

Contributors came from research institutions across Asia, North America, and Europe. The collaboration demonstrates the scientific potential of combining highly sensitive radio observations with enormous optical spectroscopy surveys.

articles.personality_title: Scientists discover why star formation is slowing despite abundant hydrogen
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Over the past 4.5 billion years, the universe has been forming fewer new stars, dropping to less than half the rate it once had. Scientists thought this might be because the fuel for stars, a type of hydrogen gas called neutral atomic hydrogen (HI), was running out.

**What happened** – An international team used China’s FAST radio telescope and data from 2.5 million galaxies observed by the DESI project to measure hydrogen levels in space. They found that while star formation dropped about 2.5 times, the amount of neutral hydrogen only fell by about 1.4 times. This means the hydrogen supply stayed mostly steady even as fewer stars formed.

**Impact** – This discovery shows that the reason for fewer stars is not just because hydrogen is disappearing. Instead, it suggests problems in how hydrogen gas turns into the denser molecular gas needed to create stars. This changes how scientists think about galaxy evolution and star formation.

**What's next step** – Researchers will now focus on understanding the gas processes inside galaxies, especially how hydrogen moves and changes form. They hope to learn why galaxies are becoming less efficient at making stars even when hydrogen is still there.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Despite plenty of hydrogen gas in space, star formation is slowing because galaxies are less able to turn that hydrogen into new stars.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les scientifiques découvrent pourquoi la formation d’étoiles ralentit malgré l’abondance d’hydrogène
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Depuis 4,5 milliards d’années, l’univers forme de moins en moins d’étoiles, à moins de la moitié du rythme d’avant. Les scientifiques pensaient que c’était parce que le carburant des étoiles, un type d’hydrogène appelé hydrogène atomique neutre (HI), s’épuisait.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Une équipe internationale a utilisé le radiotélescope FAST en Chine et des données de 2,5 millions de galaxies observées par le projet DESI pour mesurer les niveaux d’hydrogène dans l’espace. Ils ont découvert que, alors que la formation d’étoiles a chuté d’environ 2,5 fois, la quantité d’hydrogène neutre n’a diminué que d’environ 1,4 fois. Cela signifie que l’hydrogène est resté presque stable alors que moins d’étoiles se formaient.

**Impact** – Cette découverte montre que la baisse des étoiles ne vient pas seulement d’un manque d’hydrogène. Elle suggère plutôt un problème dans la transformation de l’hydrogène en gaz moléculaire plus dense nécessaire à la création d’étoiles. Cela change la façon dont les scientifiques comprennent l’évolution des galaxies et la formation des étoiles.

**Quelle est la prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs vont maintenant étudier les processus du gaz à l’intérieur des galaxies, notamment comment l’hydrogène se déplace et change de forme. Ils veulent comprendre pourquoi les galaxies deviennent moins efficaces pour fabriquer des étoiles alors que l’hydrogène est toujours présent.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – Malgré une grande quantité d’hydrogène dans l’espace, la formation d’étoiles ralentit parce que les galaxies ont plus de difficulté à transformer cet hydrogène en nouvelles étoiles.
articles.personality_title_es: Científicos descubren por qué la formación de estrellas disminuye pese a abundante hidrógeno
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En los últimos 4.5 mil millones de años, el universo ha formado menos estrellas nuevas, reduciéndose a menos de la mitad de su ritmo anterior. Los científicos pensaban que esto se debía a que el combustible para las estrellas, un tipo de hidrógeno llamado hidrógeno atómico neutro (HI), se estaba agotando.

**Qué pasó** – Un equipo internacional usó el telescopio de radio FAST de China y datos de 2.5 millones de galaxias observadas por el proyecto DESI para medir los niveles de hidrógeno en el espacio. Descubrieron que, mientras la formación de estrellas bajó unas 2.5 veces, la cantidad de hidrógeno neutro solo disminuyó unas 1.4 veces. Esto significa que el suministro de hidrógeno se mantuvo casi estable aunque se formaran menos estrellas.

**Impacto** – Este hallazgo muestra que la razón por la que hay menos estrellas no es solo porque el hidrógeno desaparece. En cambio, sugiere problemas en cómo el hidrógeno se convierte en el gas molecular más denso necesario para crear estrellas. Esto cambia la forma en que los científicos entienden la evolución de las galaxias y la formación de estrellas.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores ahora se enfocarán en entender los procesos del gas dentro de las galaxias, especialmente cómo el hidrógeno se mueve y cambia de forma. Esperan descubrir por qué las galaxias son menos eficientes para formar estrellas aunque el hidrógeno siga presente.

**Resumen en una frase** – A pesar de tener mucho hidrógeno en el espacio, la formación de estrellas disminuye porque las galaxias tienen más dificultad para convertir ese hidrógeno en nuevas estrellas.
